title: Copula Sentences
intro: Chapter 1 teaches you to say what something is with the pattern A wa B desu, and to make it negative or turn it into a question. You learn to answer yes and no, to link nouns with no, to and ka, to say "also" with mo, to point at things, places and directions, and to ask who, what, where and which. The book writes this chapter in romaji, so this file adds kana to help you start reading.

sections.title: Lessons
sections.html:
1.1 A wa B desu

This is the most basic sentence in Japanese. It means "A is B", and the same pattern also covers "I am" and "they are". A and B are nouns or noun phrases. The marker wa connects A and B and marks A as the topic, like "as for A". The ending desu is the positive, polite copula, and it never changes for I, you, he, she or they. The particle wa is written は but pronounced "wa".

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
わたしは がくせいです。watashi wa gakusei desu.I am a student.
わたしは しゃいんです。watashi wa shain desu.I am an employee.
わたしは にほんじんです。watashi wa nihonjin desu.I am Japanese.
わたしは けんしゅうせいです。watashi wa kenshuusei desu.I am a trainee.
いとうさんは せんせいです。itou san wa sensei desu.Ito is a teacher.
ADZは かいしゃです。ADZ wa kaisha desu.ADZ is a company.
すずきさんは ぶちょうです。suzuki san wa buchou desu.Suzuki is a department head.
ジェーンさんは エンジニアです。jane san wa enjinia desu.Jane is an engineer.
JLRCは がっこうです。JLRC wa gakkou desu.JLRC is a school.
マリさんは かいしゃいんです。mari san wa kaishain desu.Mari is a company employee.

1.2 A wa B dewa arimasen / ja arimasen

To say "A is not B", change desu to dewa arimasen. Another way is ja arimasen, where ja is the contracted form of dewa. Both are polite and mean the same thing. The word dewa is written では, and the は is read "wa".

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
わたしは にほんじんでは ありません。watashi wa nihonjin dewa arimasen.I am not Japanese.
わたしは エンジニアでは ありません。watashi wa enjinia dewa arimasen.I am not an engineer.
キムさんは がくせいでは ありません。kim san wa gakusei dewa arimasen.Kim is not a student.
ベンさんは けんしゅうせいでは ありません。ben san wa kenshuusei dewa arimasen.Ben is not a trainee.
やまださんは しゃいんでは ありません。yamada san wa shain dewa arimasen.Yamada is not an employee.
スミスさんは アメリカじんじゃ ありません。smith san wa amerikajin ja arimasen.Smith is not an American.
たなかさんは ぶちょうじゃ ありません。tanaka san wa buchou ja arimasen.Tanaka is not a department head.
せんせいは フィリピンじんじゃ ありません。sensei wa firipinjin ja arimasen.The teacher is not a Filipino.
マリさんは かちょうじゃ ありません。mari san wa kachou ja arimasen.Mari is not a supervisor.
すずきさんは せんせいじゃ ありません。suzuki san wa sensei ja arimasen.Suzuki is not a teacher.

1.3 A wa B desu ka

To ask "Is A B?", put the question marker ka at the end of the sentence. The word order does not change. The marker ka works like a spoken question mark, so say the sentence with a rising tone.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
せんせいは にほんじんですか。sensei wa nihonjin desu ka.Is the teacher Japanese?
ジェーンさんは エンジニアですか。jane san wa enjinia desu ka.Is Jane an engineer?
やまださんは かいしゃいんですか。yamada san wa kaishain desu ka.Is Yamada an employee?
キムさんは かちょうですか。kim san wa kachou desu ka.Is Kim a supervisor?
あなたは がくせいですか。anata wa gakusei desu ka.Are you a student?
すずきさんは けんしゅうせいですか。suzuki san wa kenshuusei desu ka.Is Suzuki a trainee?

1.4 Hai and iie: answering a yes or no question

The word hai means "yes" and iie means "no". Say hai with a positive sentence (A wa B desu) and iie with a negative one (A wa B dewa arimasen or ja arimasen). In spoken Japanese the (A wa) part is often dropped. If someone asks about "you" (anata), answer about "I" (watashi).

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
キムさんは けんしゅうせいですか。kim san wa kenshuusei desu ka.Is Kim a trainee?
はい、(キムさんは) けんしゅうせいです。hai, (kim san wa) kenshuusei desu.Yes, (Kim is) a trainee.
いいえ、(キムさんは) けんしゅうせいじゃ ありません。iie, (kim san wa) kenshuusei ja arimasen.No, (Kim is) not a trainee.
(あなたは) かいしゃいんですか。(anata wa) kaishain desu ka.Are you a company employee?
はい、(わたしは) かいしゃいんです。hai, (watashi wa) kaishain desu.Yes, (I am) a company employee.
いいえ、(わたしは) かいしゃいんじゃ ありません。iie, (watashi wa) kaishain ja arimasen.No, (I am) not a company employee.
ジェーンさんは エンジニアですか。jane san wa enjinia desu ka.Is Jane an engineer?
はい、(ジェーンさんは) エンジニアです。hai, (jane san wa) enjinia desu.Yes, (Jane is) an engineer.
いいえ、(ジェーンさんは) エンジニアじゃ ありません。iie, (jane san wa) enjinia ja arimasen.No, (Jane is) not an engineer.

1.5 Hai, sou desu and iie, chigaimasu

These are two ready-made replies that save you from repeating the whole sentence. The phrase hai, sou desu means "Yes, that's right, I agree with you", and iie, chigaimasu means "No, that's wrong, it's different". They work for any yes or no question.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
アナさんは がくせいですか。ana san wa gakusei desu ka.Is Ana a student?
はい、そうです。hai, sou desu.Yes, that's correct.
アナさんは がくせいですか。ana san wa gakusei desu ka.Is Ana a student?
いいえ、ちがいます。iie, chigaimasu.No, that's incorrect.
たなかさんは ぶちょうですか。tanaka san wa buchou desu ka.Is Tanaka a department head?
はい、そうです。hai, sou desu.Yes, that's right.

1.6 Iie, A wa C desu

In a negative answer, iie is normally paired with the negative ending dewa arimasen or ja arimasen. When you also give the correct answer, the ending becomes positive desu again, because you are now saying what is true. You can also say iie, chigaimasu first and then add the right answer.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
アナさんは がくせいですか。ana san wa gakusei desu ka.Is Ana a student?
いいえ、(アナさんは) がくせいじゃ ありません。iie, (ana san wa) gakusei ja arimasen.No, (Ana is) not a student.
いいえ、(アナさんは) かいしゃいんです。iie, (ana san wa) kaishain desu.No, (Ana is) an employee.
いとうさんは かちょうですか。itou san wa kachou desu ka.Is Ito a supervisor?
いいえ、ちがいます。ぶちょうです。iie, chigaimasu. buchou desu.No, that's not right. He is a department head.

1.7 A no B

A noun phrase is built by joining two or more nouns with a marker: noun no noun means "noun of noun" or "noun's noun", noun to noun means "noun and noun", and noun ka noun means "noun or noun". The marker no is a modifier or possessive marker. It covers belonging (my office), relationship (the president of ADZ) and description (a Japanese language student). The main noun comes last, and you can stack more than one no in a row. A sentence can also end with no to mean "A's one", as in kono kuruma wa ana san no desu.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
アナさんの ともだちana san no tomodachiAna's friend
わたしの オフィスwatashi no ofisumy office
あなたの スリッパanata no surippayour slippers
ADZの しゃちょうADZ no shachouthe president of ADZ
にほんの くるまnihon no kurumaa Japanese car
にほんごの がくせいnihongo no gakuseia Japanese language student
アナさんの にほんごの せんせいana san no nihongo no senseiAna's Japanese teacher
この くるまは アナさんのです。kono kuruma wa ana san no desu.This car is Ana's.

1.8 A to B

The marker to is an add-on marker meaning "and". It joins nouns into a complete list: A and B, and nothing else. It only joins nouns, never whole sentences.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
にほんじんと ドイツじんnihonjin to doitsujina Japanese and a German
せんせいと がくせいsensei to gakuseiteacher and student
かちょうと ぶちょうkachou to buchousupervisor and department head
にほんごと えいごnihongo to eigothe Japanese and English languages
ジョンさんと ベンさんの せんせいjon san to ben san no senseiJohn and Ben's teacher
あなたと わたしanata to watashiyou and I

1.9 A ka B

The marker ka between two nouns means "or" and offers a choice. This is a different job from ka at the end of a sentence, which makes a question. You can use both together to ask a choice question.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
にほんじんか アメリカじんnihonjin ka amerikajinJapanese or American
おとこか おんなotoko ka onnamale or female
コンピューターか カメラkompyu-ta- ka kameracomputer or camera
やまださんか すずきさんyamada san ka suzuki sanYamada or Suzuki
ぶちょうか かちょうbuchou ka kachoudepartment head or supervisor
あなたか わたしanata ka watashiyou or I
せんせいは おんなですか、おとこですか。sensei wa onna desu ka, otoko desu ka.Is the teacher female or male?

1.10 C mo B desu

The pattern C mo B desu means "C is also B". The marker wa changes to mo and takes over its topic job, so you never use wa and mo on the same noun.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
サントスさんは エンジニアです。santos san wa enjinia desu.Santos is an engineer.
スミスさんも エンジニアです。smith san mo enjinia desu.Smith is also an engineer.
ちちは かいしゃいんです。chichi wa kaishain desu.My father is an employee.
ははも かいしゃいんです。haha mo kaishain desu.My mother is also an employee.
すずきさんは せんせいです。suzuki san wa sensei desu.Suzuki is a teacher.
やまださんも せんせいです。yamada san mo sensei desu.Yamada is also a teacher.
わたしは にほんじんです。watashi wa nihonjin desu.I am Japanese.
マリさんも にほんじんです。mari san mo nihonjin desu.Mari is also Japanese.

1.11 A mo B desu ka

To ask "Is A also B?", use mo in the question. A yes answer keeps mo (hai, A mo B desu). In a negative answer, mo changes back to wa (iie, A wa B dewa arimasen or ja arimasen), because "also" is no longer true.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
アナさんも がくせいですか。ana san mo gakusei desu ka.Is Ana also a student?
はい、アナさんも がくせいです。hai, ana san mo gakusei desu.Yes, Ana is also a student.
いいえ、アナさんは がくせいじゃ ありません。iie, ana san wa gakusei ja arimasen.No, Ana is not a student.
あなたも しゃいんですか。anata mo shain desu ka.Are you also an employee?
はい、わたしも しゃいんです。hai, watashi mo shain desu.Yes, I am also an employee.
いいえ、わたしは しゃいんじゃ ありません。iie, watashi wa shain ja arimasen.No, I am not an employee.
マリさんも にほんじんですか。mari san mo nihonjin desu ka.Is Mari also Japanese?
はい、マリさんも にほんじんです。hai, mari san mo nihonjin desu.Yes, Mari is also Japanese.
いいえ、マリさんは にほんじんじゃ ありません。iie, mari san wa nihonjin ja arimasen.No, Mari is not Japanese.

1.12 kono, sono, ano + noun

Japanese has four sets of pointing words, and all of them follow the same ko, so, a, do system. The ko words are near the speaker, the so words are near the listener, the a words are far from both, and the do words are the question words. The first set is kono, sono and ano. They mean "this", "that" and "that over there", and they must always be followed by a noun. A sentence can end with no to mean "mine" or "John's", as in sono kamera wa watashi no desu.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
この かたは たなかさんです。kono kata wa tanaka san desu.This person is Mr. Tanaka.
あの くるまは ジョンさんのですか。ano kuruma wa jon san no desu ka.Is that car over there John's?
この スリッパは だれのですか。kono surippa wa dare no desu ka.Whose slippers are these?
キムさんは あの ひとです。kim san wa ano hito desu.Kim is that person over there.
この ほんは にほんごの ほんです。kono hon wa nihongo no hon desu.This book is a Japanese book.
その カメラは わたしのです。sono kamera wa watashi no desu.That camera is mine.
その ひとも がくせいですか。sono hito mo gakusei desu ka.Is that person also a student?
あの くるまは にほんの くるまです。ano kuruma wa nihon no kuruma desu.That car over there is a Japanese car.
その かいしゃは にほんの かいしゃです。sono kaisha wa nihon no kaisha desu.That company is a Japanese company.
アナさんの ノートは あの ノートです。ana san no no-to wa ano no-to desu.Ana's notebook is that notebook over there.

1.13 kore, sore, are

The words kore, sore and are mean "this one", "that one" and "that one over there". They stand alone with no noun after them, and they are used only for things, not for people or places. The same ko, so, a rule applies: kore is near the speaker, sore is near the listener, and are is far from both.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
これは アメリカの くるまです。kore wa amerika no kuruma desu.This is an American car.
あれは えいごの ほんです。are wa eigo no hon desu.That over there is an English book.
それは ジェーンさんの コンピューターです。sore wa jane san no kompyu-ta- desu.That is Jane's computer.
それは かいしゃの くるまです。sore wa kaisha no kuruma desu.That is a company car.
これは わたしの ノートです。kore wa watashi no no-to desu.This is my notebook.
それは にほんごの ほんです。sore wa nihongo no hon desu.That is a Japanese book.
あれは ジョンさんの カメラです。are wa jon san no kamera desu.That over there is John's camera.
あれは だいがくです。are wa daigaku desu.That over there is a university.
これは あねの ほんです。kore wa ane no hon desu.This is my older sister's book.
それは アナさんの スリッパです。sore wa ana san no surippa desu.Those are Ana's slippers.

1.14 koko, soko, asoko

These words point to places: koko is "here", soko is "there" near the listener, and asoko is "over there". The place word can come first (koko wa X desu) or last (X wa koko desu).

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
ここは おんなの おてあらいです。koko wa onna no otearai desu.Here is the women's washroom.
あそこは ジェーンさんの かいしゃです。asoko wa jane san no kaisha desu.Over there is Jane's company.
ここは わたしの へやです。koko wa watashi no heya desu.Here is my room.
あそこは ちゅうしゃじょうです。asoko wa chuushajou desu.Over there is the parking lot.
ジョンさんの オフィスは ここです。jon san no ofisu wa koko desu.John's office is here.
せんせいの いえは そこです。sensei no ie wa soko desu.The teacher's house is there.
かいしゃは あそこです。kaisha wa asoko desu.The company is over there.
いもうとの だいがくは そこです。imouto no daigaku wa soko desu.My younger sister's university is there.
いとうさんの いえは そこです。itou san no ie wa soko desu.Ito's house is there.
だいがくは そこじゃ ありません。daigaku wa soko ja arimasen.The university is not there.

1.15 kochira, sochira, achira

These words point to directions: kochira is "this way", sochira is "that way", and achira is "that way over there". They are also the polite way to point to a place in formal conversation. The word kochira has one more job: it introduces a person, because kore would be rude for a person.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
こちらは きむらさんです。kochira wa kimura san desu.This is Mr. Kimura.
あちらは わたしの いえです。achira wa watashi no ie desu.That way over there is my house.
そちらは わたしの かいしゃです。sochira wa watashi no kaisha desu.That way is my company.
おてあらいは そちらです。otearai wa sochira desu.The washroom is that way.
わたしの へやは こちらです。watashi no heya wa kochira desu.My room is this way.
スミスさんの オフィスは そちらです。smith san no ofisu wa sochira desu.Smith's office is that way.
だいがくは あちらです。daigaku wa achira desu.The university is that way over there.
わたしの がっこうは そちらです。watashi no gakkou wa sochira desu.My school is that way.
ちゅうしゃじょうは こちらです。chuushajou wa kochira desu.The parking lot is this way.
ベンさんの いえは あちらです。ben san no ie wa achira desu.Ben's house is that way over there.

1.16 A wa (question word) desu ka

To ask about something you do not know, put the question word where the answer would go. The sentence still ends with desu ka. The question words in this chapter are dare and donata (who), dare no and donata no (whose), nan (what), nanno (what kind of), dore (which one), dono + noun (which noun), doko (where) and dochira (which way). The word nan changes to nani when a marker follows it.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
せんせいは だれですか。sensei wa dare desu ka.Who is your teacher?
がっこうは どこですか。gakkou wa doko desu ka.Where is your school?
その おとこの かたは どなたですか。sono otoko no kata wa donata desu ka.Who is that man?
かいしゃの なまえは なんですか。kaisha no namae wa nan desu ka.What is your company's name?
アナさんの くるまは どれですか。ana san no kuruma wa dore desu ka.Which is Ana's car?
この ほんは だれのですか。kono hon wa dare no desu ka.Whose book is this?
ちゅうしゃじょうは どちらですか。chuushajou wa dochira desu ka.Which way is the parking lot?
えいごの ほんは どの ほんですか。eigo no hon wa dono hon desu ka.Which is the English book?
その ほんです。sono hon desu.That book.
その テーブルは だれのですか。sono te-buru wa dare no desu ka.Whose is that table?
この テーブルは キムさんのです。kono te-buru wa kim san no desu.This table is Kim's.
がっこうは どちらですか。gakkou wa dochira desu ka.Which way is the school?
そちらです。sochira desu.That way.
にほんごの ほんは どれですか。nihongo no hon wa dore desu ka.Which is the Japanese book?
これです。kore desu.This one.
あれは なんの かいしゃですか。are wa nanno kaisha desu ka.What kind of company is that?
あれは コンピューターの かいしゃです。are wa kompyu-ta- no kaisha desu.That is a computer company.

sections.title: Easy to mix up
sections.html:
wa and mo

  • The marker wa means "as for A", and mo means "A too". Never put both on the same noun.
  • In the question A mo B desu ka, a no answer changes mo back to wa: iie, A wa B ja arimasen.
  • The particle wa is written は but read "wa", and dewa is written では.

dewa arimasen and ja arimasen

  • The two endings mean exactly the same thing. ja is the short, casual form of dewa, and both stay polite.
  • The ending desu is positive and dewa arimasen is negative. Never say "desu dewa arimasen".

ka at the end and ka in the middle

  • At the end of a sentence, ka makes a question: nihonjin desu ka (Is he Japanese?).
  • Between two nouns, ka means "or": nihonjin ka amerikajin (Japanese or American).
  • A choice question uses both: sensei wa onna desu ka, otoko desu ka.

no, to and ka between nouns

  • The marker no means A's B, to means A and B (a complete list), and ka means A or B (a choice).
  • With stacked nouns the main noun comes last: nihongo no sensei (Japanese teacher), ana san no nihongo no sensei (Ana's Japanese teacher).
  • When no ends a sentence it means "A's one": kono kuruma wa ana san no desu.

kono versus kore

  • The words kono, sono and ano need a noun right after them: kono hon (this book).
  • The words kore, sore and are stand alone as "this thing" or "that thing": kore wa hon desu.
  • Both sets are for things. For a person say kono kata or kochira, and for a place say koko.

sono or ano?

  • The words sono, sore, soko and sochira are near the listener.
  • The words ano, are, asoko and achira are far from both of you.
  • If the thing is near you, use kono, kore, koko or kochira.

koko and kochira

  • The words koko, soko and asoko are places: koko wa watashi no heya desu.
  • The words kochira, sochira and achira are directions, and a politer way to point at a place.
  • The word kochira also introduces a person: kochira wa kimura san desu. Never use kore for a person.

dare and donata

  • The word dare is casual "who" and donata is the polite one. Add no for "whose": dare no, donata no.
  • Use donata for a teacher or someone you do not know well.

nan, nani and nanno

  • The word nan means "what". It changes to nani when a marker follows it.
  • The word nanno means "what kind of" and always sits in front of a noun: nanno kaisha (what kind of company).

dore, dono, doko and dochira

  • The word dore stands alone and means "which one" of several things.
  • The word dono needs a noun after it: dono hon (which book).
  • The word doko is "where" and dochira is "which way", and also a polite "where".

your family and my family

  • Use chichi, haha, ani, ane, otouto, imouto, sofu and sobo for your own family.
  • Use otousan, okaasan, oniisan, oneesan, otoutosan, imoutosan, ojiisan and obaasan for someone else's family.
  • The exception: you may call your own father and mother otousan and okaasan when you speak to them.
  • Never put san on your own family. Say chichi, not chichi san.

shain, kaishain, hito and kata

  • A kaishain is a company employee. A shain is an employee, often with the company name in front: ADZ no shain.
  • The words hito and kata both mean "person", and kata is the polite one: kono kata (this person), sono hito (that person).

anata and names

  • Do not use anata with a boss or someone you do not know well. Use their name plus san.
  • Put san after other people's names, never after your own.

countries, people and languages

  • Add jin for the people and go for the language: nihon, nihonjin, nihongo.
  • English is the exception: eigo, never amerikago.

hai, sou desu and iie, chigaimasu

  • The reply hai, sou desu means "Yes, that's right". The reply iie, chigaimasu means "No, that's wrong".
  • A plain iie is followed by the negative or by the right answer: iie, buchou desu.

special sounds

  • Long vowels are doubled in romaji: gakkou, sensei, otousan. Length changes the word, so practice pairs such as toki, touki and tokki.
  • A small っ holds a short pause: hakkiri, hoppeta, motta, katta.
  • A small ゃ, ゅ or ょ joins the sound before it: toukyou, gyuunyuu, myouji.
  • The sounds i and u are often almost silent: desu, kikimasu, ryuugakusei.
  • The sound n before b, m or p is pronounced like m, and some books spell it that way: shinbun or shimbun, kanpai or kampai.

sections.html:
Part A: Fill in the marker (wa, no, to, ka or mo)

#AnswerWhy
1wa (は)wa marks the topic: watashi wa.
2no (の)A no B: Ana's friend.
3to (と)to means "and" between nouns.
4ka (か)ka between two nouns means "or".
5mo (も)mo means "also" and takes the place of wa.
6ka (か)ka at the end makes the sentence a question.
7wa (は)In a no answer, mo turns back into wa.
8no (の)nihongo no hon is a Japanese-language book.

Part B: Make the sentence negative

#AnswerWhy
1watashi wa gakusei dewa arimasen. / watashi wa gakusei ja arimasen. (わたしは がくせいでは ありません。/ わたしは がくせいじゃ ありません。)Change desu to dewa arimasen or ja arimasen.
2ben san wa enjinia dewa arimasen. / ben san wa enjinia ja arimasen. (ベンさんは エンジニアでは ありません。/ ベンさんは エンジニアじゃ ありません。)Both endings mean the same thing.
3sensei wa nihonjin dewa arimasen. / sensei wa nihonjin ja arimasen. (せんせいは にほんじんでは ありません。/ せんせいは にほんじんじゃ ありません。)Only the ending changes.
4asoko wa chuushajou dewa arimasen. / asoko wa chuushajou ja arimasen. (あそこは ちゅうしゃじょうでは ありません。/ あそこは ちゅうしゃじょうじゃ ありません。)Place words work the same way.
5koko wa watashi no heya dewa arimasen. / koko wa watashi no heya ja arimasen. (ここは わたしの へやでは ありません。/ ここは わたしの へやじゃ ありません。)Keep watashi no heya together and change only desu.
6are wa daigaku dewa arimasen. / are wa daigaku ja arimasen. (あれは だいがくでは ありません。/ あれは だいがくじゃ ありません。)ja is the casual short form of dewa.

Part C: Answer each question twice, once with yes and once with no

1hai, gakusei desu. / iie, gakusei ja arimasen. (はい、がくせいです。/ いいえ、がくせいじゃ ありません。)A question about "you" gets an answer about "I", and (watashi wa) can be dropped.
2hai, kenshuusei desu. / iie, kenshuusei ja arimasen. (はい、けんしゅうせいです。/ いいえ、けんしゅうせいじゃ ありません。)You can also keep the full form: hai, (ben san wa) kenshuusei desu.
3hai, ana san mo gakusei desu. / iie, ana san wa gakusei ja arimasen. (はい、アナさんも がくせいです。/ いいえ、アナさんは がくせいじゃ ありません。)Yes keeps mo, and no changes mo to wa.
4iie, chigaimasu. buchou desu. (いいえ、ちがいます。ぶちょうです。)After a no, the right answer comes back with positive desu.
5hai, sou desu. / iie, chigaimasu. (はい、そうです。/ いいえ、ちがいます。)These two replies work for any yes or no question.

72 4 3 1: kono hon wa dare no desu ka. (この ほんは だれのですか。)Whose book is this? kono needs the noun hon right after it.

These ask about you, so the answers below are samples. Swap in your own details.

title: Existential Sentences
intro: Chapter 2 teaches you to say where things, people and animals are, and whether something exists in a place. You learn the two verbs for being somewhere, arimasu for things and imasu for people and animals, and two sentence shapes: A wa Location ni arimasu for where something is, and Location ni A ga arimasu for what is there. You also learn position words such as ue, shita and naka, and the question words doko and nani.

sections.title: Lessons
sections.html:
2.1 A wa Location ni arimasu

This pattern says that a thing is in a place. The thing (A) is the topic, so it takes wa. The marker ni points to the place where it is, and arimasu means "is" or "exists" for non-living things. The focus of the sentence is where A is, and the listener usually already knows what A is. Place words can be a name (shinjuku), a word like heya (room), or a pointing word like asoko (over there).

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
ぎんこうは あそこに あります。ginkou wa asoko ni arimasu.The bank is over there.
スーパーは あちらに あります。su-pa- wa achira ni arimasu.The supermarket is that way over there.
くるまの かぎは へやに あります。kuruma no kagi wa heya ni arimasu.The car keys are in the room.
わたしの オフィスは しんじゅくに あります。watashi no ofisu wa shinjuku ni arimasu.My office is in Shinjuku.
わたしの りょうは しぶやに あります。watashi no ryou wa shibuya ni arimasu.My dormitory is in Shibuya.
おてあらいは そちらに あります。otearai wa sochira ni arimasu.The washroom is that way.
わたしの アパートは おおさかに あります。watashi no apa-to wa oosaka ni arimasu.My apartment is in Osaka.
わたしの めがねは へやに あります。watashi no megane wa heya ni arimasu.My eyeglasses are in the room.

2.2 A wa Location ni arimasen

To say a thing is not in a place, change arimasu to arimasen. Everything else stays the same, including wa and ni.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
びょういんは あそこに ありません。byouin wa asoko ni arimasen.The hospital is not over there.
わたしの けいたいは オフィスに ありません。watashi no keitai wa ofisu ni arimasen.My cell phone is not in the office.
わたしの アパートは とうきょうに ありません。watashi no apa-to wa toukyou ni arimasen.My apartment is not in Tokyo.
えいがかんは そこに ありません。eigakan wa soko ni arimasen.The movie house is not there.
わたしの めがねは つくえに ありません。watashi no megane wa tsukue ni arimasen.My eyeglasses are not on the desk.
ほんやは そちらに ありません。honya wa sochira ni arimasen.The bookstore is not that way.
かぎは ここに ありません。kagi wa koko ni arimasen.The key is not here.
わたしの とけいは ひきだしに ありません。watashi no tokei wa hikidashi ni arimasen.My watch is not in the drawer.

2.3 A wa Location ni arimasu ka

To ask whether a thing is in a place, add ka at the end of the sentence. To ask where something is, put doko (where) in the place slot: doko ni arimasu ka. The short reply sou desu ka means "Oh, I see" when you are told something new. It is different from hai, sou desu ("Yes, that's right") from Chapter 1.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
あなたの オフィスは しんじゅくに ありますか。anata no ofisu wa shinjuku ni arimasu ka.Is your office in Shinjuku?
あなたの だいがくは とうきょうに ありますか。anata no daigaku wa toukyou ni arimasu ka.Is your university in Tokyo?
かばんは へやに ありますか。kaban wa heya ni arimasu ka.Is the bag in the room?
あなたの かいしゃは しぶやに ありますか。anata no kaisha wa shibuya ni arimasu ka.Is your company in Shibuya?
ぎんこうは あそこに ありますか。ginkou wa asoko ni arimasu ka.Is the bank over there?
あなたの くるまは いえに ありますか。anata no kuruma wa ie ni arimasu ka.Is your car at the house?
あなたの りょうは どこに ありますか。anata no ryou wa doko ni arimasu ka.Where is your dormitory?
あなたの けいたいは どこに ありますか。anata no keitai wa doko ni arimasu ka.Where is your cell phone?
りょうは どこに ありますか。ryou wa doko ni arimasu ka.Where is the dormitory?
りょうは あそこに あります。ryou wa asoko ni arimasu.The dormitory is over there.
オフィスは しぶやに ありますか。ofisu wa shibuya ni arimasu ka.Is the office in Shibuya?
いいえ、しぶやに ありません。しんじゅくに あります。iie, shibuya ni arimasen. shinjuku ni arimasu.No, it is not in Shibuya. It is in Shinjuku.
そうですか。sou desu ka.Oh, I see.
すみません、おてあらいは あちらに ありますか。sumimasen, otearai wa achira ni arimasu ka.Excuse me, is the washroom that way?
はい、そうです。あちらです。hai, sou desu. achira desu.Yes, that's right. It is that way.
いえは とうきょうに ありますか。ie wa toukyou ni arimasu ka.Is your house in Tokyo?
いいえ、いえは おおさかに あります。iie, ie wa oosaka ni arimasu.No, my house is in Osaka.

2.4 A wa Location ni imasu

This is the same shape as 2.1, but for people and animals. The verb imasu is the verb of existence for living things that move, and it is used even when you only talk about where someone is. The focus is the location of A.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
みんなは へやに います。minna wa heya ni imasu.Everyone is in the room.
ははは きっさてんに います。haha wa kissaten ni imasu.My mother is at the coffee shop.
アナさんは にほんに います。ana san wa nihon ni imasu.Ana is in Japan.
あねは ぎんこうに います。ane wa ginkou ni imasu.My older sister is at the bank.
りょうしんは アメリカに います。ryoushin wa amerika ni imasu.My parents are in the U.S.
ベンさんは りょうに います。ben san wa ryou ni imasu.Ben is in the dormitory.
かちょうは こうじょうに います。kachou wa koujou ni imasu.The supervisor is in the factory.
がくせいは きょうしつに います。gakusei wa kyoushitsu ni imasu.The students are in the classroom.

2.5 A wa Location ni imasen

To say a person or animal is not in a place, change imasu to imasen.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
アナさんは えいがかんに いません。ana san wa eigakan ni imasen.Ana is not in the movie house.
あには にほんに いません。ani wa nihon ni imasen.My older brother is not in Japan.
いとうさんは オフィスに いません。itou san wa ofisu ni imasen.Mr. Ito is not in the office.
いぬは へやに いません。inu wa heya ni imasen.The dog is not in the room.
たなかさんは ちゅうしゃじょうに いません。tanaka san wa chuushajou ni imasen.Mr. Tanaka is not in the parking lot.
わたしの ともだちは いえに いません。watashi no tomodachi wa ie ni imasen.My friend is not at his or her house.
ぶちょうは かいぎしつに いません。buchou wa kaigishitsu ni imasen.The department head is not in the conference room.
ジェーンさんは りょうに いません。jane san wa ryou ni imasen.Jane is not in the dormitory.

2.6 A wa Location ni imasu ka

To ask whether a person or animal is in a place, add ka to the imasu sentence. To ask where someone is, use doko ni imasu ka. In a reply, mo means "also": suzuki san mo doitsu ni imasu (Suzuki is in Germany too).

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
がくせいは ほんやに いますか。gakusei wa honya ni imasu ka.Are the students at the bookstore?
キムさんは ぎんこうに いますか。kim san wa ginkou ni imasu ka.Is Kim at the bank?
やまださんは オフィスに いますか。yamada san wa ofisu ni imasu ka.Is Yamada at the office?
ぶちょうは にほんに いますか。buchou wa nihon ni imasu ka.Is the department head in Japan?
ジェーンさんは カフェに いますか。jane san wa kafe ni imasu ka.Is Jane at the coffee shop?
がくせいは きょうしつに いますか。gakusei wa kyoushitsu ni imasu ka.Are the students in the classroom?
こどもは へやに いますか。kodomo wa heya ni imasu ka.Are the children in the room?
しゃいんは どこに いますか。shain wa doko ni imasu ka.Where are the employees?
たなかさんは にほんに いますか。tanaka san wa nihon ni imasu ka.Is Tanaka in Japan?
いいえ、にほんに いません。ドイツに います。iie, nihon ni imasen. doitsu ni imasu.No, he is not in Japan. He is in Germany.
ああ、そうですか。すずきさんは。aa, sou desu ka. suzuki san wa.Oh, I see. And Suzuki?
すずきさんも ドイツに います。suzuki san mo doitsu ni imasu.Suzuki is in Germany too.
やまださんは へやに いますか。yamada san wa heya ni imasu ka.Is Yamada in the room?
はい、へやに います。hai, heya ni imasu.Yes, he is in the room.
スミスさんも へやに いますか。smith san mo heya ni imasu ka.Is Smith in the room too?
いいえ、いません。かいぎしつに います。iie, imasen. kaigishitsu ni imasu.No, he is not. He is in the conference room.

2.7 Location no locative

A locative is a position word such as ue (on top), shita (under) or naka (inside). It tells the exact spot, not just the general place. Name the thing first, then no, then the position word: tsukue no ue (on top of the desk). The whole phrase works like any other place, so you can add ni arimasu or ni imasu after it. The word aida (between) needs two things joined by to: honya to ginkou no aida. The full list of position words is in the Vocabulary section.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
かばんの なかkaban no nakainside the bag
ビルの うしろbiru no ushiroback of the building
きの したki no shitaunder the tree
にほんたいしかんの まえnihon taishikan no maein front of the Japan Embassy
つくえの うえtsukue no ueon top of the desk
いえの ちかくie no chikakunear the house
ほんやと ぎんこうの あいだhonya to ginkou no aidabetween the bookstore and the bank
レストランの ひだりresutoran no hidarileft of the restaurant
くるまの かぎは つくえの うえに ありますか。kuruma no kagi wa tsukue no ue ni arimasu ka.Is the car key on top of the desk?
おとうとの がっこうは いえの ちかくに あります。otouto no gakkou wa ie no chikaku ni arimasu.My younger brother's school is near our house.
きっさてんは ほんやと ぎんこうの あいだに あります。kissaten wa honya to ginkou no aida ni arimasu.The coffee shop is between the bookstore and the bank.
スーパーは デパートの ひだりに あります。su-pa- wa depa-to no hidari ni arimasu.The supermarket is on the left of the department store.
ちゅうしゃじょうは こうじょうの まえに あります。chuushajou wa koujou no mae ni arimasu.The parking lot is in front of the factory.
ねこは へやの そとに います。neko wa heya no soto ni imasu.The cat is outside the room.

2.8 Location ni A ga arimasu

This is the second sentence shape, and it has a different job. Instead of saying where a known thing is, it says that something exists in a place, so the place comes first. The marker ga points at the thing that exists. Use arimasu for non-living things. The focus is the existence of A in that place, and A is usually new information for the listener.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
ビルの なかに レストランが あります。biru no naka ni resutoran ga arimasu.There is a restaurant inside the building.
あそこに スーパーが あります。asoko ni su-pa- ga arimasu.There is a supermarket over there.
だいがくに りょうが あります。daigaku ni ryou ga arimasu.There is a dormitory at the university.
へやに テレビが あります。heya ni terebi ga arimasu.There is a television in the room.
えきの まえに ちゅうしゃじょうが あります。eki no mae ni chuushajou ga arimasu.There is a parking lot in front of the station.
かばんの なかに けいたいが あります。kaban no naka ni keitai ga arimasu.There is a cell phone inside the bag.
へやの そとに いすが あります。heya no soto ni isu ga arimasu.There are chairs outside the room.
そこに びょういんが あります。soko ni byouin ga arimasu.There is a hospital there.

2.9 Location ni (wa) A ga arimasen

To say there is nothing in a place, change arimasu to arimasen. You can add wa after ni (ni wa) to stress the place, as if you were saying "in this place, at least, there is none". The meaning stays the same.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
へやに(は) いすが ありません。heya ni (wa) isu ga arimasen.There are no chairs in the room.
きっさてんに おてあらいが ありません。kissaten ni otearai ga arimasen.There is no washroom in the coffee shop.
ビルに ちゅうしゃじょうが ありません。biru ni chuushajou ga arimasen.There is no parking lot in the building.
りょうに(は) テレビが ありません。ryou ni (wa) terebi ga arimasen.There is no television in the dormitory.
かばんの なかに けいたいが ありません。kaban no naka ni keitai ga arimasen.There is no cell phone inside the bag.
あそこに(は) ぎんこうが ありません。asoko ni (wa) ginkou ga arimasen.There is no bank over there.
あの モールに ほんやが ありません。ano mo-ru ni honya ga arimasen.There are no bookstores in the mall.
かばんの なかに かぎが ありません。kaban no naka ni kagi ga arimasen.There are no keys inside the bag.

2.10 Location ni A ga arimasu ka

To ask whether something exists in a place, add ka. To ask what is there, use nani ga: heya no naka ni nani ga arimasu ka. The word nan becomes nani before a marker such as ga.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
かいしゃに ちゅうしゃじょうが ありますか。kaisha ni chuushajou ga arimasu ka.Is there a parking lot in your company?
テーブルの うえに ほんが ありますか。te-buru no ue ni hon ga arimasu ka.Is there a book on the table?
りょうに テレビが ありますか。ryou ni terebi ga arimasu ka.Is there a television in the dormitory?
あの えきに エスカレーターが ありますか。ano eki ni esukare-ta- ga arimasu ka.Are there escalators at that station?
あなたの がっこうに カフェが ありますか。anata no gakkou ni kafe ga arimasu ka.Is there a cafe inside your school?
つくえの うえに めがねが ありますか。tsukue no ue ni megane ga arimasu ka.Are there eyeglasses on the desk?
へやの なかに テーブルが ありますか。heya no naka ni te-buru ga arimasu ka.Is there a table inside the room?
その ビルに ぎんこうが ありますか。sono biru ni ginkou ga arimasu ka.Is there a bank in that building?
かばんの なかに なにが ありますか。kaban no naka ni nani ga arimasu ka.What is inside the bag?

2.11 Location ni A ga imasu

This is the same shape as 2.8, but for people and animals. It says that someone or something living exists in a place. The verb imasu does not change for one or many, so "there is a dog" and "there are dogs" are both inu ga imasu.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
わたしの いえに いぬが います。watashi no ie ni inu ga imasu.There are dogs in my house.
あそこに がくせいが います。asoko ni gakusei ga imasu.There are students over there.
りょうに にほんじんが います。ryou ni nihonjin ga imasu.There are Japanese at the dormitory.
へやに ねこが います。heya ni neko ga imasu.There is a cat in the room.
わたしの かいしゃに アメリカじんが います。watashi no kaisha ni amerikajin ga imasu.There are Americans in my company.
かいぎしつの なかに しゃいんが います。kaigishitsu no naka ni shain ga imasu.There are employees inside the conference room.
オフィスに かんこくじんが います。ofisu ni kankokujin ga imasu.There are Koreans at the office.
きょうしつに せんせいが います。kyoushitsu ni sensei ga imasu.There is a teacher in the classroom.

2.12 Location ni (wa) A ga imasen

To say there is nobody in a place, change imasu to imasen. As in 2.9, you can add wa after ni for emphasis.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
いえに(は) いぬが いません。ie ni (wa) inu ga imasen.There are no dogs in the house.
へやに がくせいが いません。heya ni gakusei ga imasen.There are no students in the room.
かいしゃに けんしゅうせいが いません。kaisha ni kenshuusei ga imasen.There are no trainees at the company.
へやの なかに こどもが いません。heya no naka ni kodomo ga imasen.There are no children inside the room.
あの カフェに(は) ひとが いません。ano kafe ni (wa) hito ga imasen.There are no people at the coffee shop.
きょうしつに がくせいが いません。kyoushitsu ni gakusei ga imasen.There are no students in the classroom.
オフィスに しゃいんが いません。ofisu ni shain ga imasen.There are no employees in the office.
アパートに ねこが いません。apa-to ni neko ga imasen.There are no cats at the apartment.

2.13 Location ni A ga imasu ka

To ask whether someone is in a place, add ka. To ask where someone is, use the first shape instead (doko ni imasu ka, as in 2.6). To ask who is there, use dare ga imasu ka. That question is not in your workbook, but it works the same way as nani ga arimasu ka.

JapaneseRomajiEnglish
オフィスに しゃいんが いますか。ofisu ni shain ga imasu ka.Are there employees in the office?
うちに ねこが いますか。uchi ni neko ga imasu ka.Is there a cat in your house?
かいぎしつに ひとが いますか。kaigishitsu ni hito ga imasu ka.Are there people in the conference room?
へやに けんしゅうせいが いますか。heya ni kenshuusei ga imasu ka.Are there trainees in the room?

sections.title: Easy to mix up
sections.html:
arimasu and imasu

  • The verb arimasu is for things that do not move on their own: bags, keys, buildings, tables.
  • The verb imasu is for people and animals: ana san, inu, neko.
  • Plants such as ki (tree) use arimasu, not imasu.
  • Pick the verb by what exists, not by what the sentence is about. A person's location still takes imasu: ana san wa nihon ni imasu.
  • The negatives are arimasen and imasen, and the questions add ka: arimasu ka, imasu ka.

two shapes, two jobs

  • The shape A wa Location ni arimasu answers "where is it?". The thing is already known, so it gets wa.
  • The shape Location ni A ga arimasu answers "what is there?" or "is there one?". The place comes first and the new thing gets ga.
  • The same fact can use either shape: kissaten wa honya no tonari ni arimasu (where the coffee shop is) and honya no tonari ni kissaten ga arimasu (there is a coffee shop next to the bookstore).

ni, wa and ga

  • The marker ni points at the place where something is or exists.
  • The marker wa goes after the thing you are talking about in shape one. It does not go after the place.
  • The marker ga goes after the thing that exists in shape two.
  • The words ni wa after a place only add emphasis in negative sentences: heya ni (wa) isu ga arimasen. The meaning stays the same.

where and what

  • Use doko ni for "where": ginkou wa doko ni arimasu ka.
  • Use nani ga for "what is there": kaban no naka ni nani ga arimasu ka.
  • The word nan changes to nani before a marker such as ga.
  • The question words stay in the same slot as the answer. A place goes in the doko slot, and a thing goes in the nani slot.

order inside position phrases

  • Say the thing first, then no, then the position word: tsukue no ue (on top of the desk), never ue no tsukue.
  • The word aida needs two things joined by to: honya to ginkou no aida.
  • to say exactly where something is, the whole phrase goes before ni: tsukue no ue ni arimasu.

tonari, soba, yoko, chikaku and mukou

  • The words tonari, soba and yoko all mean "beside".
  • The word chikaku means "near", so it is less exact than beside.
  • The word mukou means "across" or "on the other side".
  • The word hidari is left and migi is right. A thing on the left or right of another thing is also beside it.

look-alike words

  • The word ryou (dormitory) is not ryoushin (parents).
  • The words kissaten and kafe mean the same thing.
  • The word denwa is a phone, and keitai (denwa) is a cell phone.
  • The word kodomo is "children" or "child", and ko is the short form.
  • The words ima (now) and imasu (there is) look alike but are different words.

sou desu ka and hai, sou desu

  • The phrase hai, sou desu means "Yes, that's right". You say it to confirm something.
  • The phrase sou desu ka means "Oh, I see". You say it after you learn something new, with a rising tone.

special sounds

  • Long vowels are doubled in romaji: byouin, koujou, toshokan, kyoushitsu, ryou, ryoushin, kaigishitsu. Do not shorten them.
  • A small っ holds a short pause: kissaten.
  • Katakana long vowels use a hyphen: mo-ru, depa-to, su-pa-, apa-to, te-buru, esukare-ta-.

title: Numbers, Prices, Phone Numbers and Counters
intro: Chapter 3 teaches you to count and to talk about amounts. You learn the numbers from 0 up to hundreds of millions, how to ask for and say prices in yen, dollars and pesos, and how to read out a phone number digit by digit. You also learn the counters, which are the short endings you add when you count people, things, animals, ages and floors, such as nin, hon and hiki. Finally, you learn the question words that ask how many (nan plus the counter) and how counters fit into the sentence shapes you already know.

3.1 Numbers from 0 to 99

Japanese numbers are built like blocks. Once you know 0 to 10, you can make every number up to 99. Say the tens digit, then juu (ten), then the ones digit. So 11 is juu ichi (ten and one), 20 is ni juu (two tens), 25 is ni juu go (two tens and five) and 99 is kyuu juu kyuu. Numbers from 11 to 19 have nothing in front of juu: it is juu ichi, not ichi juu ichi.

Three numbers have two readings: 4 is yon or shi, 7 is nana or shichi, and 9 is kyuu or ku. Use yon, nana and kyuu as your safe default, because those are the ones the book uses in phone numbers and prices. The number 0 has three readings too: zero, rei and maru. The word rei also means "example", and maru also means "circle".

3.2 Hundreds

Hundreds work the same way: say the number first, then hyaku. So 200 is ni hyaku and 500 is go hyaku. On its own, hyaku is 100, with no ichi in front of it. Three hundreds change their sound, so learn them as special readings: 300 is sanbyaku, 600 is roppyaku and 800 is happyaku.

To say a number like 684, keep going from left to right: roppyaku (600), hachi juu (80), yon (4).

3.3 Thousands

Thousands follow the same idea with sen. 1,000 is sen, 2,000 is ni sen and 5,000 is go sen. Two thousands are special readings: 3,000 is sanzen and 8,000 is hassen.

The word sen turns into issen when a bigger number comes before it. That only matters from 11,000 up, as in ichi man issen (11,000). On its own, 1,000 is just sen. To say 9,713, go from left to right: kyuu sen (9,000), nana hyaku (700), juu san (13).

3.4 Ten thousands and bigger

Japanese counts in groups of four digits, not three. English has thousand and million, but Japanese has man (10,000) and oku (100,000,000). So 10,000 is ichi man (1 x 10,000), and you always say the ichi. 100,000 is juu man (ten ten-thousands), 1,000,000 is hyaku man (one hundred ten-thousands), 10,000,000 is sen man and 100,000,000 is ichi oku.

3.5 Prices: ikura desu ka

To ask a price, use ikura (how much): A wa ikura desu ka. To ask for a rough price, add gurai (about): A wa ikura gurai desu ka. To answer, say the number and then the currency: en (yen), doru (dollars) or peso (pesos). So 180 yen is hyaku hachi juu en.

The phrase zenbu de means "in total, for all of it together". It goes at the front of the sentence: zenbu de ikura desu ka. To check a price, say the amount and add ka, like any yes or no question: sanbyaku go juu en desu ka. 3.6 Phone numbers: denwa bangou wa nan desu ka

To ask for a phone number, say denwa bangou wa nan desu ka (what is it?) or denwa bangou wa nanban desu ka (what number is it?). For a cell phone, use keitai bangou. Both questions mean the same thing in everyday use.

To say the number, read every digit on its own. Never group them like "eighty-four". Say no for the hyphen. A zero can be zero, rei or maru, so pick one and keep it. Use yon, nana and kyuu for 4, 7 and 9, as the book does. For example, 7326-5471 is nana san ni roku no go yon nana ichi.

3.7 Counters

In Japanese you do not just say "three apples". You add a counter, which is a short ending that depends on what you are counting. This chapter teaches tsu (anything), sai (age), nin (people), mai (thin, flat things), hon (long, thin things), satsu (books and notebooks), kai (times), kai (floors of a building), ko (small things), hiki (small animals), dai (machines and vehicles) and ban or banme (order, such as which child you are). Pages use the counter pe-ji. The number and the counter join into one word: san plus ko is sanko.

There are two ways to use a counter with a noun. You can say the noun and then the counter, as in ringo sanko, or the counter, then no, then the noun, as in sanko no ringo. Both mean three apples.

Some counters change their sound with certain numbers, mostly 1, 3, 6, 8 and 10 (ippon, sanbon, roppon, happon, juppon). People have special readings for 1, 2 and 4 (hitori, futari, yonin). 3.8 Counters in sentences

Counters fit into the sentences you already know. With desu, the sentence says what the count is: A wa counter desu, as in otouto wa hatachi desu (my younger brother is 20). In the second shape, the counter sits right in front of the verb, after the thing and its ga. Use imasu for people and animals, and arimasu for things. In this file the number and counter are written as one word (juugonin, sanbyakunin, sanjuugosai). To ask how many, put nan in front of the counter: nannin (how many people), nanbon (long things), nansatsu (books), nanbiki (small animals), nandai (machines and vehicles), nanmai (flat things), nanko (small things), nankai (how many times), nangai (what floor) and nanbanme (which number in a family or line). For things counted with tsu, and for age, use ikutsu (how many things) and oikutsu (how old, polite). The word nansai also asks for age.

sections.title: Easy to mix up
sections.html:
Numbers with two readings

  • The number 4 has two readings, yon and shi. The number 7 has nana and shichi. The number 9 has kyuu and ku.
  • When you are unsure, use yon, nana and kyuu. Every phone number and price in this chapter uses them.
  • People are the one place to watch: 4 people is yonin, and 7 people is shichinin or nananin.

Special hundreds and thousands

  • Only 300, 600 and 800 change: sanbyaku, roppyaku and happyaku. The other hundreds are plain: ni hyaku, yon hyaku, go hyaku, nana hyaku and kyuu hyaku.
  • Only 3,000 and 8,000 change: sanzen and hassen. The other thousands are plain: ni sen, yon sen, go sen, roku sen, nana sen and kyuu sen.
  • 100 is hyaku and 1,000 is sen, with no ichi in front. Say ichi only before man and oku: ichi man, ichi oku.

Sen and issen

  • Say sen when 1,000 stands alone or starts the number: sen, sen go hyaku (1,500).
  • Say issen when a bigger number comes first: ichi man issen go hyaku (11,500).
  • Quick check: if there is a man in front of it, the word is issen.

Big numbers with man and oku

  • Think in groups of four digits, not three. 10,000 is ichi man, not juu sen.
  • 100,000 is juu man (10 x 10,000), not hyaku sen. 1,000,000 is hyaku man and 10,000,000 is sen man.
  • 100,000,000 is ichi oku.
  • A quick trick is to cut the number into fours from the right. 24,200,560 becomes 2420 and 0560, so you say ni sen yon hyaku ni juu man, then go hyaku roku juu.

Reading phone numbers

  • Read digit by digit. 8434 is hachi yon san yon, never "eighty-four thirty-four".
  • Say no for the hyphen.
  • A zero can be zero, rei or maru. All three are fine, so pick one.
  • denwa bangou wa nan desu ka and denwa bangou wa nanban desu ka both ask for the number.

Sankai and sangai

  • The ending kai is written the same for times and floors, but the sound for 3 differs: 3 times is sankai and the 3rd floor is sangai.
  • For 1, 6, 8 and 10 the two meanings sound the same: ikkai, rokkai, hachikai or hakkai, and jukkai. The sentence tells you which one is meant.
  • The question words differ too: nankai asks how many times, and nangai asks what floor.

Which counter to use

  • People take nin. Small animals take hiki. Machines and vehicles take dai. Books and notebooks take satsu.
  • Thin, flat things take mai, for example paper, tickets, stamps and letters.
  • Long, thin things take hon, for example pencils, pens, bottles and umbrellas.
  • Small things take ko, for example apples and oranges.
  • When you are unsure, the general counter tsu works for many things, up to 10.
  • Age takes sai. Floors and times both take kai. Order or rank in a family takes ban or banme.

Sound changes to drill

  • The counters shift mostly on 1, 3, 6, 8 and 10. With hon: ippon, sanbon, roppon, happon, juppon. With hiki: ippiki, sanbiki, roppiki, happiki, juppiki.
  • With ko the changes are ikko, rokko, hakko and jukko, but sanko stays plain.
  • With satsu the changes are issatsu, hassatsu and jussatsu. The rest are plain.
  • The numbers 2, 4, 5, 7 and 9 stay plain: nihon, yonhon, gohon, nanahon, kyuuhon.
  • People are special on 1, 2 and 4 only: hitori, futari, yonin. After that they are plain: sannin, gonin, rokunin.

Ikura, ikutsu and nan plus a counter

  • ikura asks about a price. ikutsu asks how many things. nan plus a counter asks how many of one kind: nannin, nanbiki, nandai.
  • For age, oikutsu is the polite question and nansai is also fine.
  • Before a counter it is nan, never nani. Say nannin, not naninin.
  • ikura gurai asks for a rough price. The word gurai means about.

Two ways to place a counter

  • Noun then counter: ringo sanko. Counter, no, then noun: sanko no ringo. Both mean three apples.
  • The word no joins the counter to the noun, so use it only when the counter comes first.
  • In the sentence shape Location ni A ga counter imasu, the counter sits between ga and the verb: gakusei ga futari imasu.

Imasu or arimasu with counters

  • People and animals take imasu: gakusei ga futari imasu, inu ga sanbiki imasu.
  • Things take arimasu: ringo ga itsutsu arimasu.
  • The verb does not change with the number. imasu stays imasu for one dog or ten.

Hatachi and other ages

  • Age 20 has its own special word, hatachi. Learn it as a separate word.
  • Ages 1, 8 and 10 shift their sound: issai, hassai and jussai.
  • Other ages are the number plus sai, for example sanjuugosai (35). oikutsu and nansai ask the question.

Yen, dollars and pesos

  • Say the amount first, then the currency: sen en, go hyaku doru, ichi man peso.
  • The book writes doru as do-ru in one example, but the word is doru.
  • Check a price with the amount and ka: sanbyaku go juu en desu ka. Reply with hai, sou desu or iie, chigaimasu.

#AnswerWhy
1ani ga hitori, ane ga hitori, otouto ga futari imasu. (あにが ひとり、あねが ひとり、おとうとが ふたり います。)People take nin and imasu. hitori and futari are the special readings for 1 and 2 people. ani, ane and otouto are older brother, older sister and younger brother in your own family.

8watashi wa sanbanme desu. (わたしは さんばんめです。)banme gives the order, so 3rd is sanbanme.
9kippu wa sen roppyaku ni juu en desu. (きっぷは せんろっぴゃくにじゅうえんです。)1,620 is sen roppyaku ni juu. roppyaku is the special reading for 600.
